messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Writer
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan is a 20-year-old South Asian American writer who presented for treatment approximately seven months after the sudden death of his younger brother, Arjun, who collapsed without warning from an undetected cardiac arrhythmia during a family gathering. Arjun was seventeen. There had been no illness, no warning, no moment in which the family could have prepared themselves. One moment Arjun was laughing at the dinner table; the next, Rohan was on the floor beside him, calling his name while their mother screamed for someone to dial 911. Rohan held his brother's hand until the paramedics arrived. Arjun was pronounced dead at the hospital that evening.

In the weeks that followed, Rohan described feeling as though the architecture of his understanding of the world had simply collapsed. He had grown up believing, in the way that most young people do without examining it, that catastrophe announces itself — that there are signs, that youth is a kind of protection, that the people sitting across from you at dinner will still be there tomorrow. Arjun's death had not simply taken his brother; it had dismantled every quiet assumption Rohan had ever made about how life worked. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt less like a thought and more like a physical fact, that the world was genuinely and randomly dangerous — that safety was an illusion people told themselves because they had not yet seen what he had seen. When friends described feeling safe or content, he found their confidence bewildering, almost naïve.

Rohan had always identified as a warm, curious, and essentially happy person. Writing had come easily to him; he had been working on a novel and contributing essays to a small literary magazine. In the months after Arjun's death, he found himself certain that the person who had written those pages no longer existed. He did not experience this as grief in any form he recognized — he experienced it as a permanent alteration, a before and after with no bridge between them. He was not sad in a way that felt temporary. He was miserable in a way that felt like the truth about him now.

His sleep had deteriorated significantly. He lay awake for hours, and when he did sleep, he woke easily. Ordinary sounds — a door closing in another room, a notification chime from his phone, a car backfiring outside his apartment building — would jolt him upright, his heart pounding, his body certain something had gone wrong. He was unable to settle even in environments he knew to be safe. Sitting at his writing desk, which had once been a place of absorption and pleasure, he found himself scanning, waiting, unable to release the vigilance that had taken up residence in him since the night he knelt on the floor beside his brother.

His writing had effectively stopped. He could not make plans — not for the novel, not for submissions, not even for the following week. What frightened him most about planning was the implicit assumption that the future would arrive, that the people he loved would be in it. He had learned, in the most visceral way possible, that this assumption could be shattered in a single moment, and he was not willing to make it again. He had withdrawn from a writing residency he had been accepted to before Arjun's death, citing personal reasons without elaborating. His editor at the literary magazine had stopped reaching out after several unanswered emails.

He had also begun seeking reassurance from his parents and his closest friend with a frequency that had begun to strain those relationships — asking, repeatedly, whether they thought he was handling things normally, whether they believed he would be all right. He avoided anything that carried Arjun's presence: a particular playlist, the restaurant where they used to eat together, the neighborhood where they grew up.

What finally brought Rohan to seek help was a conversation with his mother, who told him quietly that she was worried she was losing him too. He came to the first session saying very little about what he hoped for, except that he wanted to know whether it was possible to live in the world again without being afraid of it.
